client: I've been really struggling since my partner moved abroad for work six months ago. It feels like no matter how many video calls we have, there's this growing distance between us that I can't seem to bridge. I'm honestly not sure talking to a therapist is going to fix the fact that they're just... not here.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that video calls can't fully replace the warmth of someone being physically present — that ache you're feeling is a very real and valid grief, not just a mindset problem to be "fixed." I also hear a little skepticism about whether talking can help, and I think that's worth honoring rather than brushing aside. 

I'm curious — when you notice that feeling of distance most strongly, what tends to be going through your mind in those moments?

client: It's usually the small stuff that gets me — like when something funny happens during my day and I want to share it immediately, but by the time we're on a call, the moment's just gone. I start thinking, "what's the point, they're building a whole new life over there and I'm just... stuck here." And then I feel guilty for even thinking that, like I'm being selfish or unsupportive.
therapist: That image of a funny moment evaporating before you can share it is such a tender, specific kind of loneliness — it makes perfect sense that it would trigger those bigger fears about growing apart. I want to gently point something out: you called yourself "selfish" for missing your partner and feeling left behind, but I'm wondering if you'd use that same word if a close friend described feeling exactly the way you do right now?

client: No, I wouldn't call a friend selfish for that — I'd probably tell them their feelings make total sense. But it feels different when it's me, like I should be stronger or more understanding because I knew this move was coming and I agreed to it. So using the same compassion on myself just feels... kind of hollow, like I'm letting myself off the hook for something.
therapist:
You've just noticed something really important — that you hold yourself to a completely different, much harsher standard than you'd hold someone you love, and that self-compassion feels like a loophole rather than something you genuinely deserve. That belief that "I agreed to this, so I shouldn't struggle" is worth examining, because agreeing to something difficult doesn't cancel out the very human experience of finding it hard. 

What do you think "being strong enough" would actually look like to you — what would you be feeling, or not feeling, if you were doing this "right"?

client: I think "doing it right" would look like being busy and fulfilled on my own, not really minding the distance, maybe even seeing it as an opportunity for personal growth or whatever. I wouldn't be lying awake at night replaying old memories or checking their social media to see what their new life looks like without me in it. Saying it out loud like that, it does sound kind of impossible, like I've set a standard that nobody could actually meet.
therapist:
You just did something really powerful — you held that standard up to the light and saw it clearly for what it is, almost like a rule that sounds reasonable until you say it out loud. It's worth noticing that the version of "doing it right" you described sounds less like a person in love and more like someone who simply doesn't care very much.

What do you think it would mean about your relationship if the distance *didn't* bother you?

client: I guess if it didn't bother me at all, that would probably mean I'd already checked out of the relationship in some way. And I hadn't really thought about it like that before — that the pain is actually connected to how much I care. But I'm not sure that realization actually makes the loneliness easier to sit with, you know? It still feels like a long time to just... wait.
therapist:
You're absolutely right that understanding *why* something hurts doesn't make it stop hurting — insight and relief aren't the same thing, and it's important not to skip over that. But I want to gently push back on one word: "wait" — because that framing positions you as someone on pause, and I wonder if there's a version of this time that feels less like waiting and more like something else entirely.

What would it look like to be *living* through this period, rather than waiting for it to end?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me likes the idea of reframing it that way, but honestly it also feels a little like I'd be betraying the relationship somehow — like if I get too comfortable and start building my own full life here, I'm accepting that this distance is okay when it's really not. And I'm also just not sure what "living through it" would even look like practically, because most of the things I used to enjoy, I used to do with them.
therapist:
That fear of "getting too comfortable" is really worth sitting with, because it reveals a belief that suffering is somehow proof of loyalty — as if staying a little miserable keeps the relationship real and present. And the practical piece is just as important; it's genuinely hard to rediscover what brings you joy when so much of your joy was woven together with another person, and that's not a personal failing, it's just where you are right now.

Can you think of even one small thing — something tiny — that you used to enjoy before this relationship that got quietly set aside along the way?

client: There was this thing I used to do on Sunday mornings — I'd go to this little independent bookshop nearby and just browse for an hour with no particular goal, maybe get a coffee. I kind of stopped because it felt like something we were supposed to discover together eventually, like I was saving it. But now that I say that, I realize I've been holding onto these little experiences like they're not really mine to have on my own, which is a strange way to live.
therapist:
That image of "saving" experiences like they belong to the relationship rather than to you is such a revealing and honest thing to notice — and it sounds like somewhere along the way you started to feel like *you* needed to be put on hold too. That bookshop hasn't gone anywhere, and neither has the part of you who loved it.

I wonder what it might feel like to walk in there this Sunday — not as a betrayal, not as "moving on," but just as a small act of being present in your own life?

client: I think I actually want to try that, which surprises me a little because usually when someone suggests something like this I find a reason why it won't work. But I'm already noticing this small voice saying "you should tell your partner first, get their approval somehow," and I'm not sure if that's me being considerate or me just needing permission to exist independently again.
therapist:
That small voice is worth listening to carefully, because you've named something really profound — there's a difference between *sharing* something with your partner out of love and *needing their permission* to feel allowed to be yourself. The fact that you noticed that distinction on your own, in real time, suggests you already know which one this is.

What do you think it would mean for you — and for the relationship — if you went to that bookshop simply because *you* wanted to, and told your partner about it afterwards with joy rather than asking first?

client: I think it would mean I'm starting to trust that the relationship can hold me being a full person, not just someone who's paused and waiting. But there's still this fear that if I start enjoying things independently, we'll grow in different directions and have even less in common when they come back. I know that probably sounds like I'm looking for reasons to stay stuck, but it feels like a real risk to me.
therapist:
That fear isn't you looking for reasons to stay stuck — it's a genuinely understandable worry, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than argued away. But I want to offer a gentle alternative thought: two people who are each growing, living fully, and bringing new experiences back to each other often have *more* to share, not less — whereas two people on pause can find they've quietly drifted apart without either of them even moving.

What does your partner moving abroad and building a new life there tell you about what *they* believe the relationship can hold?

client: That's actually a really uncomfortable question because when I flip it around like that, I have to admit that my partner didn't put their life on hold — they took the job, they're making friends, they're exploring a new city. And I've never once thought of that as them being disloyal or not caring enough, so there's something pretty unfair about the way I've been treating myself compared to them. I think I needed someone to point that out, even if it stings a little to sit with it.
therapist:
That sting you're feeling is actually the sound of a really important belief starting to shift, and it takes courage to let yourself see something that clearly even when it's uncomfortable. You've essentially uncovered a rule you've been living by — that your partner is allowed to be fully alive out there, but you're not allowed to be fully alive in here — and now that you can see it, you get to decide whether you want to keep following it.

As you sit with all of this, what feels most different about how you're seeing yourself and this situation compared to when we first started talking today?
